title: BIO144 Course Information (version 2027, draft)
text:
Preface
This website contains information about the BIO144 Data Analysis in Biology course at the University of Zurich.
Beware that Owen sometimes makes updates to the information during the semester, so if you have downloaded a copy or taken screenshots, your copy may not exactly match the most current version. If content changes in an important way Owen will make an announcement on OLAT, or by email.

title: BIO144 Course Information (version 2027, draft)
text:
How this website was made
The website was written using a type of RMarkdown. It allows a script with a mix of normal text and R code to produce chapters and a book that has a mixture of text, R code, and R output. Rmarkdown is very useful for making reports, books, presentations, and even websites.
This book is a Quarto book. To learn more about Quarto books visit https://quarto.org/docs/books.

title: General information
text:
Aims and learning outcomes
This course will help you develop a solid foundation in answering biological questions with quantitative data. Moreover, the approaches you will learn are generally applicable to using data to solve problems, an increasing important skill in a world more and more dominated by data.
The Learning Objectives of the course tell you what you need to learn and know. Hence, it is very important for you to be very clear about the learning objectives of the course. They will help you know what you’re expected to learn and what you will be examined on. If you can achieve all of the learning objectives, you will be very well prepared for a great future in data analysis (and for the exam).

title: General information
text:
Course schedule
The course runs during the spring semester. The course has 12 weeks of new content, and some weeks with no new content (the Easter break, and weeks for self-study, review and catch-up; see the detailed schedule). Each of the 12 weeks of new content has a set of learning objectives. Each week has four parts: a lecture, homework, a practical session, and a practice quiz.
Lectures are on Monday mornings, 8:00 - 9:45. Practical sessions are on Thursday or Friday afternoons, 13:00 - 14:45.
You’ll be assigned to a practical session on either Thursday or Friday. If at any point you wish to change afternoons permanently, contact studienkoordination@biol.uzh.ch. If you want to swap days for just one or two weeks, please do so without asking.
Please see the “Year specific information” section below for a detailed course schedule.
Please note that the day of the last practical session in the last week of the course (usually the last Friday of the semester; see the detailed schedule) is the last day that we can guarantee that you will be able to get help with any problems you have with the course content. After that, we will not be available to help you with content-related questions. We of course remain available to answer questions about the examination arrangements.

title: General information
text:
Expected workload
The course is worth 4 credit points, so with 1 CP being approximately 30 hours work, requires around 120 hours study. Approximately one third of this is “in class” and two thirds is self-study, including in-course assessments and preparation for the examination.

title: General information
text:
Bring your own laptop
Please bring your laptop to class. There are some power outlets in the lecture theatre, but best will be to make sure that your laptop has sufficient battery charge to last the duration of the class (up to 2 hours), and consider using an external additional battery (powerbar?) if required. Please make sure you know how to use your laptop (some people are sometimes not so sure, perhaps because its new.) Your laptop must be able to connect to the wireless internet at UZH.

title: General information
text:
Software
You can use R and RStudio either on your own laptop or through a web browser on the UZH RStudio Server (see below). The final exam uses RStudio Server, so whichever you choose, make sure you can log in to RStudio Server and work there. If you want to work on your own laptop, please make sure you have these programmes:

A spreadsheet programme, such as Microsoft Excel, Apple Numbers, or OpenOffice.
The R software environment for statistical computing and graphics.
Rstudio. We use RStudio to interact with R. Rstudio has lots of features that make working with R much much easier and enjoyable.

If you need any help setting up your laptop with R and RStudio, please look at the “Getting R & RStudio” section of the BIO144 Previous Knowledge self-tests (see the Previous knowledge chapter for more). If you still have problems, no worries… ask for help during the first practical.

title: General information
text:
RStudio server
You can use RStudio Server during the course instead of (or as well as) R and RStudio on your own laptop, and you will have to use it in the final exam. Access it at https://rstudio.mnf.uzh.ch/ and log in with your UZH username and password. The Unit 1 practical starts by checking that everyone can log in.

title: General information

What to do each week

Attend the lecture.
After the lecture and before the practical do the homework.
Come to and do the practical.
Do the practice quiz.
Have fun ;)

title: General information
text:
Course texts
The required content of the course is all available in the course book: BIO144 Course Book. The lectures will help you understand the content of the book. The homework and practicals will also help you learn the material. Practice quizzes will help you check your learning, and prepare for the final exam. All of this will also help you develop your skills in R, which will also be required in the final exam.
There is other optional reading that we may suggest to you during the course. This is listed below. Textbooks for optional reading are in the main library, and should be accessible electronically through the main library.
Optional reading comes from the following books. Also each chapter of the course book suggest reading to further your understanding.

Linear Regression, Seminar für Statistik, ETH Zürich(2008 / 2013) Werner Stahel. And here is an English version of that text.
Getting Started with R, An introduction for biologists (2017, Second Edition) Beckerman, Childs & Petchey. (DO NOT USE THE FIRST EDITION!). The link is to the book on the Oxford University Press website; full access to the book will require you have a UZH ip address (i.e. are on the UZH network or VPN into it).
Insights from Data with R, by Petchey, et al. (Same access information as the previous book in this list).
The New Statistics with R, An Introduction for Biologists (2015, First Edition) Hector. Ebook via UZH library.

Some other nice (though optional) texts that you might find interesting.

Regression; Models, Methods and Applications (2013 Edition) Fahrmeir, Kneib, Lang & Marx.
The Analysis of Biological Data (2015, Second Edition) Whitlock & Schluter.
The Essential Guide to Effect Sizes. Statistical Power, Meta-Analysis, and the Interpretation of Research Results (2010, First Edition) Ellis. Ebook via UZH library.
Statistics: An Introduction using R (2011, Second Edition) Crawley.

title: General information
text:
Getting datasets
Various datasets are used in the course.
Datasets used in the homework and practicals are all in one place: the practical datasets folder (this is “the usual place” mentioned in the practicals). You can download them all at once as a zip file, which you will then need to unpack before use. Most practicals also show you code to download the dataset you need straight into your RStudio project.
Datasets used in the course book are available in a different zip file, which is provided in the course book (Preface).
Datasets associated with the book Getting Started with R, by Beckerman, Childs, and Petchey here.
IMPORTANT: if you open the downloaded file in Excel, perhaps to have a look at it, then DO NOT, UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES, ASK OR ALLOW EXCEL TO SAVE IT. (Excel does not like R and will do everything in its power to mess things up for R. Don’t let it do that.)

title: General information
text:
Attendance
Attending class is a really good idea!:
“attendance [is] a better predictor of college grades than any other known predictor of academic performance”,
Credé, Roch, & Kieszczynka, 2010. The full article.
We give you the freedom to use the learning materials and opportunities in the way that suits you best. We strongly believe that attending the practical classes and lectures will be an efficient, fun, and valuable way for you to learn.
We will not be tracking attendance. If you do not come to class (practical or lecture) the only penalty you will potentially experience is loss of some learning opportunity.
What if I was ill or otherwise unable to attend? Please use your initiative to catchup. Lectures will be available as podcasts. Ask for help from friends for help with practicals. And whatever else you can think of.

title: General information
text:
Assessment
There will be two assessment-related types of activity:

1. Weekly practice quizzes
These are only for you. Your scores do not contribute to anything. The are intended:

To make sure you know if you’re learning and understanding the material.
To motivate you to keep up with the content of the class, and thereby reduce the chance of you falling behind and then having trouble in the final exam.
To give you practice with the types of questions that will be in the final examination.

There is no deadline for the practice quizzes. You can do them whenever you like. You can do them multiple times if you like.


2. The final exam (and the resit exam)
A final assessment during the module examination period. Your performance in this is the only determinant of your final grade.
Examination date and time: Please see the Studium Biology, Modulprufungen im Grundstudium web page and the links therein for the examination dates and other important examination information.
This information is for 2027.
The BIO144 final exam and resit are governed by the programme level regulations that can be found on this web page: https://www.biologie.uzh.ch/de/Studium/Bachelorstudium/Grundstudium/modulpruefung.html
In addition:

The exam will contain about 40 questions. Each will be one of three types: single choice, multiple choice, or numeric. Single choice is a question with several possible answer, of which only one is correct – you indicate which. Multiple choice is a question with several possible answers; none, 1, 2, 3, or 4 may be correct – you indicate which. Numeric requires you to enter a number to answer the question.
A mock exam will be available on OLAT. The mock exam is intended to give you experience with the types of questions that will be in the final examination. It will be similar in terms of the types of questions and structure, and is intended to be similar in difficulty.
During the exam you are allowed three sheets of A4 paper that you may put information on both sides of. You can write on these sheets whatever you like, and they can be printed or handwritten. Do not bring more than three sheets of A4 paper. The limit is number of pieces of paper, not number of sides of paper that you put information on.
You are allowed to bring into the exam one translation dictionary (Übersetzungswörterbuch) (e.g., an Englisch–Deutsch-Wörterbuch / English–German dictionary). Examination staff should be allowed to inspect this resource.
You will need to present your UZH card during the exam, to verify your identity.
You will take the exam on your laptop.
You will need to use your laptop continuously during the two hours of the exam. Some power outlets are available, but best is to make sure you have enough battery power to last the exam.
Your laptop must connect to the internet via wifi.
You will take the exam in a special instance of OLAT from within the Safe Exam Browser that must be installed on your computer.
From within the Safe Exam Browser you will be able to use RStudio Server.
RStudio Server will, during the exam, be configured in “exam mode”. You will not have access to your normal home folder. Access to your normal home folder will be restored after the exam. Rstudio Server will be configured so that Copilot cannot be used. You will be able to query and read R help files (e.g., using ‘?lm’ to get help on the ‘lm’ function).
There will be a mandatory practice exam experience including use of the Safe Exam Browser. Details will be sent to you.
The exam is in English.
You must agree with an Honour Code on OLAT immediately before you take the exam.
You will sit the exam in a lecture theater on the Irchel Campus.
The final exam requires you to analyse some datasets that are provided to you. Some students have reported that they didn’t have enough time during the exam, so please ensure that you can do things like importing data quickly and easily.
Your working (e.g. any R code your write) is not assessed directly. It is assessed indirectly by whether you answer a question correctly.
During the exam, if you have any trouble importing the data, please immediately ask for help.
When answering numeric questions, the default is to give your answer with precision of 2 decimal places. Some questions specify to give the answer to a different number of decimal places. Please be careful to take care of this.
You are allowed to use your phone when authenticating login to the exam environment and to RStudio server, but you are not allowed to use your phone for anything else during the exam. Phone use will be very carefully monitored.

title: General information

Getting help
We aim that you can ask for help about anything and get a useful answer as soon as possible. The following guidelines will help you get fast and useful help. The primary ways to ask for help are:

During the practicals on Thursday and Friday.
Anytime on the Discussion Forum of this OLAT course. We aim that you get a response in less than two days. Anonymous posts are possible.
During and after lectures.

Of course, please feel free to email Owen directly if you wish (but he may ask you to post on the Forum if he feels that would be better). Please don’t hesitate to ask for help!

Posting code problems on the Discussion Forum
The Wiki:FAQ contains a page How to ask a question so we can easily help. Please take a look.


Specialist statistical assistance
I (Owen) am not a statistician. Hence, I might be unable to answer some of your questions about more statistical issues, particularly as we experience more and more complex statistics. To deal with this, Prof. Furrer has agreed to help with about statistics that I cannot answer (or cannot answer fully). Please post them as a new thread in the discussion forum. Include as much information as possible, including R code and output as appropriate. Please do not contact Prof. Furrer directly. We will then contact Prof. Furrer and feedback the answer to you.

Your views on the course are really important to us. What works well, what doesn’t work so well, what content is particularly important, what content is not so important, what content is missing?

During the course, you can tell us in person during class, and can make posts on the Forum. Such feedback during the course has the potential to improve the course for you. I.e., we might be able to change something quickly, so your and your fellow students’ experience of the class is improved.

Probeprüfung (Practice exam experience)
In mid to late May there will be a mandatory practice exam experience. This is to make sure that you can use the system that will be used for the final exam, and to give you experience with it.
The most important aims of the Probeprüfung are:

Check you can use the Safe Exam Browser on your computer, and if not to fix any issues before the examination.
Check that you can log in to the exam environment.
Check that you can log in to RStudio server from within the exam environment.

Please note that you can do 1. and 2. independent of the Probeprüfung, and you are encouraged to do so. You can make a SEB-Testlauf with details here. You can make a SEB Funktionstest with details here – search for BIO144.
ZI information about online exams – very useful for you to read and understand.

Required wifi network
In the final on-site exam you should use a UZH-network (“uzh” or “uzh-5ghz”) because these are the most reliable. Therefore, to best replicate final exam conditions, it is recommended to use these networks also for the Probeprüfung. If you wish to not use one of these for the Probeprüfung (e.g., so you can be off-site for the Probeprüfung), everything should still work.


Passkeys for authentication

Therefore, passkeys have to be removed for UZH-Login (Rstudio) & edu-ID-Login (OLAT). Please see the section below for instructions on how to do this (you must remove them from both accounts, UZH-Login and edu-ID-Login, and in both cases you must remove them in your authenticator app and on the Microsoft website).


Phone use during real exam
You are allowed to use your phone when authenticating login to the exam environment and to RStudio server, but you are not allowed to use your phone for anything else during the exam. Phone use will be very carefully monitored.


Check that you can use the Safe Exam Browser
The Probeprüfung involves you starting the Safe Exam Browser (SEB) by clicking on a link in a website. If this works correctly the SEB will start up and you will be presented with log in prompt.
Things that can go wrong, and possible solutions:

You may have clicked the wrong link. Try again, and make sure you click the correct link.
You may be told your SEB version is wrong. If so, update your SEB to the required version and try again. More info can be found here SEB installation
You may have some other issue… contact ZI Support for help.



Check that you can log in to the exam environment
After the SEB starts, it should open and prompt you to login with your Switch Edu-ID credentials. Do this.
Things that can go wrong, and possible solutions:

You may have entered the wrong username or password. Try again, and make sure you enter the correct username and password.
After you enter your username and password, a window opens and the process of authenticating starts but then stalls. This is probably caused by you having a passkey configured. See below for detailed instructions on how to fix this issue.
You may have some other issue… contact ZI Support for help.



Check that you can log in to RStudio server from within the exam environment
Once logged in you will see the exam environment where you must first confirm that you have read the Ehrenkodex. Only after you confirm the Ehrenkodex can you start the exam. Once you start the exam, you will see 40 questions. In each question there is a link to RStudio. It is very important that you check that you can log in to RStudio server from within the exam environment, and if not to fix any issues before the examination.
Things that can go wrong, and possible solutions:

The exam won’t start. Check that you have confirmed the Ehrenkodex. If not, do so and try again.
The username and or password you use to log in to RStudio server is not recognised. The username and password are NOT the same as your Switch Edu-ID username and password. Try again, and make sure you enter the correct username and password. These are the username and password you use to log in to your email.
After you enter your username and password, a window opens and the process of authenticating starts but then stalls. This is probably caused by you having a passkey configured. See below for detailed instructions on how to fix this issue.

How to fix the issue of authentication stalling when trying to log in to RStudio server from within the exam environment
Login to OLAT and RStudio in Safe Exam Browser will not work if you have a passkey configured for your UZH Microsoft account.
Before making any changes, always ensure that you have at least one backup authentication method available. Otherwise you may lock yourself out of your account.
You can check your authentication methods here (outside SEB, in a normal browser): https://mysignins.microsoft.com/security-info
Additional UZH instructions for MFA setup are here: https://www.zi.uzh.ch/en/support/Outlook-und-Kollaboration-Office-365/setup-multifactor-authentification.html#Set_up_Multifactor_Authentication
Then follow these steps:

Select the University of Zurich UZH account.

Select Delete passkey.
Confirm deletion of the passkey.

Next, also check that no passkeys remain configured in your Microsoft account:

Open https://mysignins.microsoft.com/security-info
Review the listed authentication methods.
Remove any remaining passkeys associated with your UZH account.

Then:

Restart the mock exam from the exam overview page.
Try logging in to RStudio again.

title: Previous knowledge
text:
What you should already know
Many of you already have skills and knowledge that are important for data analysis in biology, from previous learning – in particular, if you have taken them, from MAT183 (Stochastik für die Naturwissenschaften) and from BIO134 (Programming in Biology). This chapter covers what you should already know, and why.
You’ll greatly benefit from having a reasonable recall of this material, and this chapter is meant to help with that. None of it is mandatory, but it’s likely to be very useful. Here are some things you might benefit from doing before the first class:
Please note that this chapter is not exhaustive – there might be other things you’ve previously learned that are also useful for BIO144.

title: Previous knowledge
text:
From MAT183 – Stochastik für die Naturwissenschaften

Methods for describing characteristics of some data. For example, measures of where the centre of the data is (e.g. mean, median, mode), measures of the spread of the data (e.g. quartiles, variance, standard deviation, standard error), and measures of the symmetry of the spread (e.g. skew). Also kurtosis, i.e. how “peaked” a distribution is, and when we’d say a distribution is bimodal.
The definition of, and the difference between, a population and a sample.
Basic use of R and RStudio, including basic arithmetic on scalars and vectors, use of logical operators (<, >, ==, !, &, |), importing data into R, and getting basic summary information about your data (e.g. mean, median, variance, standard deviation).
Basic probability. For example, what is the probability of getting five heads if we toss a fair coin seven times? What is the probability that, given a couple has three children, at least two are boys?
The importance and characteristics of a few probability distributions: normal, binomial, Poisson, exponential. Many methods of data analysis require at least a basic understanding of these. You will have worked with these distributions in R, using functions such as dnorm(), pnorm(), qnorm(), and rnorm().
Frequency distributions (histograms) are important for visualising the distribution of your data. You should know what these are and how to make them in R, e.g. using the hist() function.
As well as histograms, you should know when and how to make box-and-whisker plots, QQ-plots, and bivariate scatterplots.
The statistical concepts: expectations, parameters, parameter estimates, the central limit theorem, hypothesis testing, and standard error of the mean.
A few basic statistical tests: the one- and two-sample t-tests, and the chi-squared test. You should know when to use them, what they can tell us, and how to implement them in R.



From BIO134 – Programming in Biology
In BIO134 you spent a lot of time learning concepts and practices of programming, using the language Python. In BIO144 you’ll use a different language, R (via RStudio), which you’ll already have used a bit in MAT183. There are lots of similarities between Python and R, so it’s worth applying what you learned in BIO134 in this class (though there are also differences, so don’t expect your Python code to work unchanged in R!). For example, you’ll benefit from recalling what you learned about functions, strings, files, plotting, and data analysis such as Spearman correlation. You’ll also have learned that accuracy really matters when coding – a single wrong character can have very unwelcome consequences.


Other prior knowledge
This will be useful to review before the course starts, but will also be recapped during it.

The equation of a straight line.
Types of variable: numeric, continuous, discrete, categorical, dependent, independent, explanatory, response.

title: Previous knowledge
text:
Notation
An overview of the notation used throughout the course is in the “Notation and some definitions” section of Chapter 1 of the course book. Most of it is also conventional statistical notation you’ll have seen elsewhere. If you have questions about it, use the Discussion Forum, or ask during the first or second practical (i.e. before lecture 3, when we start using it).

title: Previous knowledge
text:
Checking and practising this material
To check your recall of the material above, and to get set up with and comfortable using R and RStudio, work through the BIO144 Previous Knowledge self-tests. It has:

Self-tests covering the topics above: basic statistics, distributions, probability distributions, data visualisation, important terms and concepts, and basic statistical tests.
Getting R & RStudio: help installing R and RStudio, if you don’t have them already.
Getting to know R: a short walkthrough of the very basics of using R, with a script to follow along with.
Help about R and RStudio: how to get help when you’re stuck, and some recommended books.
What are add-on packages?: what add-on packages are, and how and when to install and load them, including the tidyverse.

None of the self-tests there are graded – they’re just for you, to help you see what you remember well and what’s worth reviewing before the course starts.

title: Learning Objectives
text:
Course-level learning objectives
This document describes the learning objectives for BIO144: Data Analysis in Biology.
The learning objectives describe what you must be able to do, and so what could appear in the exam. As well as the learning objectives, the content of each chapter of the course book is “must know”.
After successfully completing BIO144, students will be able to:

title: Learning Objectives
text:
Translate a biological question into a statistical model by identifying the response variable, the explanatory variables and the structure of the data.
Choose an appropriate model (linear model, generalised linear model, mixed model or ordination) for a given question, type of response variable and study design, and justify the choice.
Explain degrees of freedom, calculate them for the models used in the course, and work out the residual degrees of freedom expected from a planned study design and model before the data are collected.
Use R and RStudio to import, explore, manipulate and visualise biological data in a reproducible script.
Fit these models in R and obtain parameter estimates, their uncertainty, predictions and hypothesis tests.
Use diagnostics to evaluate whether model assumptions are reasonably met, and judge the consequences of violations for the conclusions.
Interpret model results quantitatively and in biological terms, focusing on effect sizes and their uncertainty rather than on p-values alone.
Evaluate whether an analysis supports a stated biological claim, recognising limitations such as correlation versus causation, extrapolation and pseudoreplication.
Recognise clear, correct and complete reporting of statistical results in text, tables and figures.

title: Learning Objectives
text:
Unit-level learning objectives

Introduction (Chapter 1)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Describe how the lectures, course book, practicals, homework, weekly quizzes and final exam of BIO144 fit together. (not examined)
Identify the prior knowledge and skills assumed at the start of the course, and where to revise them. (not examined)
Describe the steps of a data analysis workflow, from formulating a question to communicating the answer, and explain why the presentation and analysis should be planned before the data are collected.
Describe the four principles for high-quality data analysis: a focused question with planned sampling and analysis; a model that accounts for the distribution and dependence of the data; emphasis on effect sizes and biological relevance; and reporting that makes the research reproducible.
Explain the advantages of doing a data analysis with a script in R, such as being repeatable, readable and sharable.
Distinguish appropriate from inappropriate uses of AI assistants in learning data analysis and in BIO144 assessments.
Recognise and use the course notation for samples, populations and linear models (e.g. the sample mean, sample and population standard deviation, parameter estimates and residuals).



R and RStudio (Chapter 2)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Explain the purpose of the script, the console and the environment in RStudio.
Write and run R code in a script, using objects, functions and arguments correctly.
Install and load add-on packages, and explain the difference between installing and loading a package.
Use R’s help system and other resources to find out how a function works and what arguments it takes.
Import a dataset into R and inspect its structure, including the variable names and variable types.
Convert variables to factors, and set or change the reference level of a categorical variable.
Manipulate data in R: select variables, filter observations, create new variables, and calculate summaries by group.
Produce exploratory graphs (e.g. histograms, scatterplots, box plots) to inspect distributions of and relationships between variables.
Identify and fix common errors in R code (e.g. typos, misspelled variable names, packages not loaded).
Organise an analysis as a script within an RStudio project, with meaningful names for datasets and model objects, that reproduces all results when run from top to bottom.



Simple linear regression – Part 1 (Chapter 3)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Explain when simple linear regression is an appropriate tool for a biological question.
Write the simple linear regression model as an equation, and identify the intercept, slope and error term.
Explain the least squares principle by which the intercept and slope are estimated.
Calculate fitted values and residuals from a regression equation and data.
Explain what degrees of freedom are: the number of independent pieces of information left for estimating variation after the model parameters have been estimated, so that the residual degrees of freedom equal the number of observations minus the number of estimated parameters.
Explain why the residual variance of a simple linear regression is estimated by dividing the residual sum of squares by n − 2, and calculate the residual degrees of freedom.
Explain why few residual degrees of freedom are a problem: imprecise estimates of the residual variance, larger critical t-values and so wider confidence intervals and less power, a risk of fitting noise, and difficulty checking assumptions.
Describe how the error term is modelled: normally distributed, with mean zero and constant variance.
State the assumptions of simple linear regression.
Use R to fit a simple linear regression with lm() and obtain the estimated intercept and slope.
Use diagnostic plots to judge whether the assumptions of a linear regression are reasonably met, and identify which assumption is violated if not.
Explain leverage and Cook’s distance, and identify influential observations.
Identify common problems in a regression (e.g. non-linearity, non-constant variance, influential observations) and select an appropriate remedy (e.g. a transformation).
Interpret the coefficients of a regression with a log-transformed response and/or explanatory variable (e.g. as proportional or multiplicative effects).
Explain what makes a model linear (linear in its parameters), so that models with transformed variables can still be fitted with lm().



Simple linear regression – Part 2 (Chapter 4)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Explain what the correlation coefficient (r) and R² each measure, and how they differ.
Explain R² as the proportion of the total sum of squares explained by the model, and calculate it from the sums of squares.
Use R to obtain r and R² for a simple linear regression, and interpret their values.
Identify the null hypothesis tested by the t-test of a regression slope.
Explain what a p-value is, and calculate the t-statistic of a slope as its estimate divided by its standard error.
Explain how the number of degrees of freedom changes the t-distribution, and why fewer residual degrees of freedom give wider confidence intervals and larger p-values for the same t-statistic.
Use R to test whether the estimated slope is compatible with zero or another specified value, and draw the appropriate conclusion.
Use the residual degrees of freedom (n − 2) to obtain the critical t-value for a confidence interval and the p-value for a slope, and identify the degrees of freedom in R output.
Use R to obtain a 95% confidence interval for the slope and intercept, and interpret it.
Distinguish a confidence band from a prediction band, and explain why the prediction band is wider.
Use predict() to calculate the expected value of the response, with its confidence interval or prediction interval, for a new value of the explanatory variable.
Interpret the slope and intercept in the biological units of the study, including whether the intercept is biologically meaningful.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of regression results that reports the estimate, its uncertainty and the test result.
Evaluate whether a regression analysis supports a stated biological claim, considering R² versus statistical significance, extrapolation beyond the data, model diagnostics, and correlation versus causation.



One-way ANOVA (Chapter 5)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Explain one-way ANOVA as a linear model with a single categorical explanatory variable.
Explain how the total variation is partitioned into between-group and within-group components, and how the F statistic is calculated from them.
Calculate the total, model and residual degrees of freedom of a one-way ANOVA (n − 1, k − 1 and n − k), and explain why they add up.
Explain why sums of squares are divided by their degrees of freedom to give mean squares, and identify the two degrees of freedom of the F-distribution.
Calculate missing entries in an ANOVA table (degrees of freedom, sums of squares, mean squares, F).
Use R to fit a one-way ANOVA with lm() and obtain the ANOVA table.
Use R to test whether the group means differ, and draw the appropriate conclusion.
Interpret the coefficients of a model with a categorical explanatory variable: the reference level and the differences from it.
Use R to obtain group means and the estimated differences between groups, with their uncertainty.
Use diagnostic plots to judge whether the assumptions of a one-way ANOVA are reasonably met.
Explain why testing many pairs of groups inflates the probability of a false positive, and use a correction for multiple comparisons (e.g. Bonferroni, Tukey HSD).
Decide whether one-way ANOVA is appropriate for a described study design and response variable.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of one-way ANOVA results.



Multiple regression (Chapter 6)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Identify biological questions that require a model with more than one explanatory variable.
Write the multiple regression model as an equation, and explain what each coefficient represents.
Use R to fit a multiple regression with lm().
Use diagnostic plots to judge whether the assumptions of a multiple regression are reasonably met.
Calculate the model and residual degrees of freedom of a multiple regression, counting k − 1 degrees of freedom for a categorical explanatory variable with k levels, and use them in the F-test and in adjusted R².
Use the overall F-test to judge whether the explanatory variables together explain variation in the response.
Interpret each coefficient as the association between that explanatory variable and the response with the other explanatory variables held constant, including its direction and size.
Use R to obtain R² and adjusted R², and explain why adjusted R² is needed when comparing models with different numbers of explanatory variables.
Compare the importance of explanatory variables measured on different scales using standardised coefficients, and explain what is lost by standardising.
Use predict() to make predictions for given values of all explanatory variables.
Explain what collinearity is, detect it (e.g. correlations among explanatory variables, variance inflation factors), and describe its consequences for coefficient estimates and their uncertainty.
Use the residual degrees of freedom of two nested models in an F-test comparing them.
Explain what a confounding variable is, how including a measured confounder in a multiple regression reduces bias in the estimated effect of another variable, and why this cannot prove causation.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of multiple regression results.



Interactions (Chapter 7)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Explain what an interaction between two explanatory variables means, both biologically and in the model equation.
Distinguish additive from interactive effects using graphs of data or of model predictions.
Explain why one model with several explanatory variables (and their interaction) is preferable to several separate single-variable analyses.
Use R to fit models with interactions between two categorical variables (two-way ANOVA), a categorical and a continuous variable (ANCOVA), and two continuous variables.
Interpret interaction coefficients, including how the meaning of the main-effect coefficients changes when an interaction is in the model.
Use R to calculate and plot how the effect of one explanatory variable depends on the value of another.
Test whether an interaction is needed, and judge whether it is biologically meaningful.
Calculate the degrees of freedom of main effects and interaction terms, and the residual degrees of freedom, from the number of parameters a model estimates.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of results from a model with an interaction.



Generalised linear models for count data (Chapter 8)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Identify biological questions and study designs in which the response variable is a count.
Explain why linear models with normal errors are often inappropriate for count data (counts are non-negative integers, and their variance tends to increase with the mean).
Describe the three components of a generalised linear model: the linear predictor, the distribution family and the link function.
Use R to fit a Poisson regression with glm().
Explain null and residual deviance as measures of fit for a GLM, analogous to sums of squares in a linear model.
Check the assumptions of a Poisson GLM using diagnostic plots, recognising that QQ-plots of deviance residuals are interpreted differently from those of a linear model.
Interpret coefficients on the log (link) scale, and back-transform them to multiplicative effects on the expected count.
Use R to calculate predicted counts for given values of the explanatory variables.
Use deviance-based tests to judge whether explanatory variables are associated with the response.
Explain that in a chi-squared (likelihood ratio) test between nested GLMs, the degrees of freedom equal the difference in the number of estimated parameters.
Detect overdispersion and select an appropriate response to it (e.g. a quasi-Poisson or negative binomial model).
Recognise zero inflation in count data, and that it requires models beyond the Poisson GLM.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of results from a Poisson regression.



Generalised linear models for binary data (Chapter 9)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Identify binary response variables (e.g. presence–absence, success–failure) in described biological studies.
Distinguish individual-level binary data from aggregated binomial data (number of successes out of a number of trials).
Explain why linear regression on proportions, or Poisson regression on the number of successes, is unsuitable for binary and binomial responses.
Explain the logit link and the relationship between probability, odds and log-odds.
Convert between probabilities, odds and log-odds.
Use R to fit a logistic regression with glm().
Use R to fit a binomial GLM to aggregated data, specifying the numbers of successes and failures.
Interpret coefficients as changes in log-odds, and back-transform them to odds ratios.
Use R to calculate predicted probabilities and plot the fitted relationship.
Use deviance-based tests to judge whether explanatory variables are associated with the response.
Check a binomial GLM before interpreting it, using the GLM checklist, and recognise which checks are hard to interpret for individual-level 0/1 data.
Use the ratio of residual deviance to residual degrees of freedom to check aggregated binomial data for overdispersion, use a quasibinomial model as a pragmatic fix, and recognise that this check is not informative for individual-level binary data.
Recognise separation in a logistic regression from its symptoms (e.g. very large coefficient estimates and standard errors).
Recognise a correct and complete statement of results from a logistic regression.



Ordination and multivariate data (Chapter 10)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Recognise when a biological question involves many response variables, and explain the limitations of analysing each one separately.
Reshape multivariate data between wide and long format, and explain which format is needed for which task.
Explain the aim of ordination: to summarise similarity among observations measured on many variables using a few axes.
Explain why variables are centred, and usually scaled, before a PCA.
Use R to perform a principal component analysis (PCA) and obtain the proportion of variation explained by each axis.
Interpret PCA loadings and biplots to identify which variables contribute most to each axis.
Choose a distance measure for NMDS appropriate to the data (e.g. Euclidean distance on scaled numeric variables).
Use R to perform a non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) and obtain its stress value.
Interpret ordination plots in terms of similarities and differences among observations.
Distinguish PCA from NMDS, and choose between them for a given dataset.
Evaluate what an ordination does and does not show (e.g. it summarises patterns but does not by itself test hypotheses; tests need separate methods).
Choose an appropriate approach to test whether groups differ in multivariate composition (MANOVA, PERMANOVA) and in multivariate spread (PERMDISP), and to relate an explanatory variable to an ordination (envfit, ordisurf).
Use principal components as explanatory variables in a regression, as one way to deal with collinearity.



Mixed models (Chapter 11.1)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Recognise grouped, nested or hierarchical data in biological study designs (e.g. repeated measures, individuals within populations, sites within regions).
Explain why ignoring grouping in the data leads to pseudoreplication and overconfident conclusions.
Explain why averaging the repeated measurements within each group before using lm() is sometimes acceptable but often throws away information.
Recognise pseudoreplication when a model’s residual degrees of freedom are much larger than the number of independent units (e.g. individual plants) in the study.
Distinguish fixed effects from random effects, and decide which is appropriate for a variable in a described study.
Distinguish random intercept models from random slope models, and nested from crossed random effects, and write the corresponding lmer() formula.
Explain partial pooling, and how it shrinks group-level estimates towards the overall mean.
Use R to fit linear mixed models with random intercepts, and with random slopes, using lmer() from the lme4 package.
Use R output to obtain the fixed-effect estimates and the variance components.
Interpret mixed model output in biological terms, including what the variance components say about variation among groups.
Explain why degrees of freedom, and so p-values, for fixed effects in mixed models are not straightforward, and that several approximations exist (e.g. Satterthwaite’s method).
Identify limitations and assumptions of mixed models in a described analysis.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of results from a mixed model.



What next? (Chapter 11.2)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Describe which kinds of data the methods in BIO144 can analyse: data that meet the assumptions of linear models, count and binary data using generalised linear models, grouped or repeated-measures data using mixed models, and many variables at once using ordination.
Explain why data collected over time or across space often violate the assumption of independent observations, and so require specialised methods (time series analysis, spatial analysis).
Recognise features of a research question or dataset that call for methods beyond BIO144, such as non-independent observations, non-linear relationships, abrupt changes in a relationship, many interrelated variables, time-to-event responses, or results from multiple studies.
Match a described research situation to a suitable family of methods: time series analysis, spatial analysis, non-linear regression, breakpoint analysis, generalised additive models, structural equation modelling, machine learning, meta-analysis, survival analysis, non-parametric methods, power analysis or Bayesian statistics.
Explain why the analysis, including the sample size needed (power analysis), should be planned when the study is designed.
Explain why the choice of analysis should be driven by the research question rather than by the techniques available.



Review: planning and implementing statistical analyses (Chapter 12)
After this unit, students will be able to:

Write a planning sentence for a described study, stating the question, the type of response variable, the data structure, the explanatory variables, the planned model and the expected residual degrees of freedom.
Choose a model (linear model, binomial GLM, Poisson GLM, mixed model or ordination) from the type of response variable, the explanatory variables and the data structure of a described study.
Identify the experimental unit in a described study, and recognise pseudoreplication.
Explain the roles of replication, randomisation, controls, blocking and balance in study design.
Count the parameters a planned model will estimate, calculate the expected residual degrees of freedom, and judge whether they are enough.
Explain how sample size affects the precision of estimates and the power of a study, and what a power analysis is for.
Decide which terms to include in a model from the question and the design (variables of interest, planned interactions, design variables, potential confounders), and explain why trying many models or using stepwise selection gives misleading p-values.
Check a fitted model before interpreting it, make explicit predictions from it, and plot the predictions together with the data.
Recognise a report that gives both the statistical result and its biological meaning.

How to ask a question so we can easily help?
You’re probably quite competent at asking questions so that we can easily help. But here are a few tips that can help you be even better:

If you’re asking a question in the OLAT Forum and include R code, please try to ensure it is easy to read and copy into R.
If you’re asking for help about some code that doesn’t work, please consider making a “minimal, reproducible example”. This web page describes what one is and how to make one (https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example).



Is practical attendance mandatory?
You are free to do the practicals whenever you want, but we encourage that you do attend the practical afternoons, especially if you have questions!


Can I change which practical afternoon I attend?
In general it’s better that you stick to the afternoon you registered for, but if you cannot attend it you can of course join the practical on the other day.


Are the sections named Extras part of the exam?
No, they are just for your interest!


Device with enough battery for exam
If you are not certain that the battery of your laptop can last for the duration of the final examination, please let us know using the form at the end of the course content here on OLAT.


About the Discussion Forum
Use the discussion forum to ask questions, give tips, make suggestions about how the course could be improved… or anything else that springs to mind while you’re taking the course.
However, before posting please check this FAQ page to see whether your question has already been answered, and also look at the other forum posts to see whether there is already a discussion thread for your topic. If you cannot find what you are looking for, go ahead and post something in this forum, we will respond as soon as possible!
Other potential uses of the forum are that you may make a list of questions that you want to ask during the class, or a list of things that you’d like us to go over again in class, or in more detail in lectures or practicals. Then we can look at these in lectures or practicals.
One rule: do not post complete solutions to exercises. Help others find and realise for themselves the answer, but don’t post the actual answer. This may include deleting or editing your post.
Another rule / guideline. Open a new post / thread for a new issue.

text:
R-related FAQ

What version of R is needed?
It is good practice to keep R up to date, so it is recommended that you have the most recent version of R installed. In any case, you should at least have the R version 4.0 or newer installed. You can check the version by running “version” or “sessionInfo()” in R.


What packages are needed?
The packages needed in each unit are loaded with library() in the course book chapter and in the practical. The main ones are:

tidyverse (contains ggplot2, readr, dplyr, tidyr, forcats, and others)
ggfortify (diagnostic plots with autoplot())
car (variance inflation factors with vif())
multcomp (Tukey multiple comparisons)
GGally (ggpairs())
lme4 and lmerTest (mixed models)
vegan (ordination)

On the UZH RStudio Server most of these are already installed. On your own computer, install each one once with install.packages().


I am having issues installing a package
Problems with installing packages are somewhat common. Often, these problems be avoided by using
install.packages( "NAME", type = "binary")
instead of simply
install.packages( "NAME", )
The reason is that quite often, packages are available a source packages, which must be compiled locally, which is often not possible on standard R machines. Therefore, by specifying type = “binary”, you tell R to install the already compiled version, even though it might be an older version.


My output of summary(), str() etc. looks different from older materials
Older materials (books, web pages, older videos) sometimes show output that looks a bit different from what you get. Usually the reason is that, since R version 4.0.0, text columns are read in as character (<chr>) variables rather than factors, and functions such as summary(), glimpse() and str() show character variables differently from factors. Package updates can also change how output looks. In BIO144 we use read_csv() from the readr package, which reads text columns as character variables. That is fine: linear models work with character variables as well as factors (see “Should I convert character variables to factors?” below).


What does rm(list=ls()) do? Should I use it?
rm(list=ls()) deletes all the objects in R’s environment (ls() lists their names and rm() removes them). You will see it at the top of many older scripts, including some older BIO144 materials.
In BIO144 we now recommend something better: restart R (Session > Restart R in RStudio) and run your script from the top. Restarting gives a completely fresh R session: it also unloads packages and resets options, which rm(list=ls()) does not. If your script then runs from top to bottom without errors, you know it does not depend on anything you did outside the script. Working in an RStudio project (see the Unit 1 practical) helps too.


How do I set the number of decimal places shown?
Use the round() function to tell R how many decimal places to report and what rounding to do. You otherwise cannot know for sure how a number displayed in the console has been rounded or not.


What does the predict() function do?
In general, the predict() function takes as argument a model object, for instance one fitted with lm(). It then predicts/estimates/calculates the response variable based on the values of the covariates (explanatory variables) and the estimated coefficients according to the fitted model. You can do this by hand (good for understanding).
If you do not specify the data to use for the prediction, it will automatically use the data that was used in fitting the model. You can also specify the dataset used, which is useful, for instance when you have multiple covariates and you want to visualize the relation of one specific explanatory variable with the response variable. In that case you create a new dataset in which you keep every covariate at constant values (e.g. their mean) with the exception for the one in you are interested in. Then you can use this dataset in the predict() function and then, if you want, you can plot the relation of that variable with the response.
Note: predict() does not fit a model, it evaluates a model with some given data


What does the expand.grid() function do?
The expand.grid() function is a handy function to create new data, as it returns every possible combinations of the input provided. For instance expand.grid(a = 1:2, b = 4:5) returns
    a b
1   1 4
2   2 4
3   1 5
4   2 5

We often use this function to create new data because we want to visualize the effect of one particular variable on the response variable according to the fitted model. When we have a model with more than 1 explanatory variable, these variables can vary together and if they do the effect of one particular variable on the response variable is more difficult to see. Hence to best show the importance of a particular variable, we keep all other variables at constant values. These constant values should ideally be sensible values, i.e. keeping the mass at 0 does not make sense, but it makes more sense to keep at the mean value.


Which diagnostic plots does autoplot() show?
By default, autoplot() (from the ggfortify package) shows four diagnostic plots for a linear model: residuals vs fitted values, the normal QQ-plot, the scale–location plot, and residuals vs leverage. You can choose which plots to show with the which argument, as with plot() for linear models:
autoplot(my_model, which = 1:6)   # all six plots
autoplot(my_model, which = 4)     # Cook's distance for each observation
When a model has only categorical explanatory variables, all observations in a group have the same leverage, so the residuals vs leverage plot is replaced by a plot of residuals against the factor levels. That’s fine: the other plots are the more important ones.
Note that autoplot() does not work for mixed models (lmer()): use plot(my_model) for the residuals vs fitted values, and qqnorm(resid(my_model)) for a QQ-plot.


gather() vs pivot_longer() and spread() vs pivot_wider()
Some older materials (and many older web pages) use the tidyr functions gather() and spread(). These have been replaced by pivot_longer() and pivot_wider(), which are easier to use. In BIO144 we use pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() (see the course book, Chapter 2).


unique() vs levels()
The function levels() only works with factors. read_csv() reads text variables as characters, not factors, so levels() gives NULL for them. Use unique() instead of levels() to see the different values of a character variable.


Should I convert character variables to factors?
read_csv() reads text variables (e.g. country, continent) as characters (chr), not factors. Linear models work with both, so you do not have to convert them. The main reason to convert a variable to a factor is to set the order of its levels (e.g. for a graph, or to choose the reference level; see the next question). If you do want to convert one variable:
dd <- dd |> mutate(continent = factor(continent))
And to convert all character variables at once (not usually needed):
dd <- dd |> mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))


How do I change the reference level of a categorical variable?
In summary() of a linear model, the coefficients of a categorical variable are differences from the reference level, which by default is the first level in alphabetical order. To use a different reference level, for example “control”, use fct_relevel() from the forcats package (loaded with the tidyverse), then fit the model again:
dd <- dd |>
  mutate(treatment = fct_relevel(treatment, "control"))
The model is the same model (the fitted values and the anova() table do not change), but the coefficients and their t-tests in summary() now compare each level with “control”. See the course book, Chapters 5 and 7.


Plotting one regression line when the points are coloured by group
Question: I map colour = continent in ggplot(), and geom_smooth() then draws a separate regression line for each continent. How do I get one line for all the data, with the points still coloured by continent?
Answer: Aesthetic mappings given in ggplot() are inherited by all the geoms, so geom_smooth() also uses colour = continent. Put the mapping only in the geom that needs it:
ggplot(health_data, aes(x = log10_expenditure, y = log10_mortality)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = continent)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
(Alternatively, keep the mapping in ggplot() and remove it from the smooth with geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(colour = NULL)).)


ggpairs() shows too many graphs. Can I show only some variables?
Yes: select the variables you want first, then make the graph:
bodyfat_data |>
  select(bodyfat, age, abdomen, height, weight) |>
  ggpairs()


How do I find the extreme values of each variable?
To see the row with the largest value of one variable, use slice_max() (and slice_min() for the smallest):
dd |> slice_max(abdomen, n = 1)
Note that the largest value is not necessarily an extreme value: it may be perfectly in line with the other values. One common definition of an extreme value (used for the points shown separately in box plots) is a value more than 1.5 times the interquartile range below the first quartile or above the third quartile. Graphs (histograms, box plots, scatterplots) are usually the best way to spot extreme values.

title: FAQs
text:
Statistics-related FAQ

What is the difference between fitted and predicted values?
Fitted values: The response values you get when you use the observed values of the explanatory variables, i.e. the ones you used to fit the model: the original data
Predicted values: In general, the response values you get when you use new observations of the explanatory variables (i.e. new data). Note: if the new data is the same as the original data, then predicted values == fitted values.
This being said, it happens that the terms fitted values and predicted values are used interchangeably, even though there is a (small) difference.


Interpretation of p-values
The p-value is best interpreted as:
The p-value is the probability of having a test statistics value at least as extreme as the value actually observed (e.g. the t-value of the t-test or F-value of the F-test) given that the Null hypothesis is correct (often H0: parameter=0). If the p-value is below 0.05 we reject H0 and go with H1 (often H1: parameter =/= 0). The p-value is not the probability of H0 being correct.
See also the lecture material.


Interpretation of confidence intervals
Let’s assume we have a simple linear regression with body-fat as the response and BMI as the explanatory variable. We find that the slope of BMI is 1.75 with a corresponding 95% confidence interval [1.55,1.97]. This is interpreted as follows:

“All true values for beta1 (slope for BMI) between 1.55 and 1.97 are compatible with the observed data”.
To rephrase this slightly, this means: the true slope for BMI could have any value between 1.55 and 1.97 and we would not be surprised to see the data that we have (and thus, if the true slope was outside the interval, it would be surprising to see the data that we have: the estimated slope based on the data does not match the true slope.

Note: I want to stress that it is not correct to say that there is a 95% probability that the true slope is between 1.55 and 1.96 (see below).
So, with the interpretation given above, if the confidence interval of the slope does not cover 0, then a slope of 0 is not compatible with the data. In fact, in the case of the 95% confidence interval this means that the p-value is below 0.05, which means that we reject the Null hypothesis H0 that the slope for BMI is 0. Note: this is neither “good” nor “bad”, it is just what it is: we are just interested in the truth.
There is an alternative interpretation of confidence intervals which is arguably more precise (but you can use the above for this course). To explain it, here are a couple of things that I personally think are good to keep in mind:

The parameter of interest (e.g. the slope of BMI) is estimated based on the available data, meaning that the estimate is a function of the data. If for instance the experiment is repeated the data will look a little bit different and the estimate will be a little bit different. However: the true value of the parameter of interest (the slope) is the same in both experiments!
The same thing goes for confidence intervals: they are estimated based on the data, so if the data changes a bit, the upper and the lower bound of the confidence interval will be a bit different as well.
An example of wrong interpretation: continuing the example above, let’s say we know the true slope of BMI and it is 2. What is the probability that the confidence interval includes the true slope? 0 (!), because 2 is not in [1.55,1.97]. And what would the probability be if the true slope is 1.6? 1 (!), because 1.6 is included in [1.55,1.97]. This is why it is incorrect to say that there is a 95% probability that the estimated confidence interval contains the true slope: the estimated confidence interval either contains or it does not contain the true slope.

Now, because of probability theory reasons, a confidence interval is best interpreted like this:

“If we repeat the entire experiment many times (and thus collect slightly different data each time) and for each experiment we calculate the 95% confidence interval, then 95% of the calculated confidence intervals will contain the true parameter value”.
This definition is a bit harder to get, but it basically tells us that it is a measure of uncertainty of the estimated slope.



Model diagnostics residuals versus fitted values
The central assumption of linear regression is that the errors are independent (from each other) and identically distributed (i.i.d.) following a normal distribution with mean = 0 and variance = sigma^2. We cannot measure the errors directly, but we have estimates of them: the residuals. This means that we can check these assumptions based on the residuals, because given that they are estimates of the errors and that the model is valid the residuals have to be i.i.d. following a normal distribution as well. In the figure residuals vs. fitted values we can check for some of these assumptions:

Mean = 0: the mean has to be zero across all fitted values. So the points in the figure have to be spread approximately symmetrically above and below 0, so that the mean is approximately 0 across all fitted values. If for instance we see that for larger fitted values the mean of the residuals increases or decreases clearly away from 0, then this assumption might be violated.
Variance == sigma^2: constant variance. Similarly to above, the variance has to be independent from the fitted values, meaning that the spread of point below and above 0 needs to be approximately the same across all fitted values. If this is not the case this results in a pattern (e.g. larger fitted values result in a higher variance in the residuals) and this assumption might be violated.



Difference between binomial and count data
For count data we use Poisson regression and for binomial data we use binomial regression (commonly called logistic regression)

Count data come from questions like “how many times have you voted in your life?” and the answer can be a positive integer (including 0), while binary data come from questions like “did you vote last year?” to which the answer can only be yes (1) or no (0).
We get binomial data if we have n (=number of persons) independent Bernoulli trials (i.e. binary trials), so we would basically count how many people have voted last year out of the n we asked. In other words, if we have 7 yes and 3 no to the question “did you vote last year?”, they come from 10 different people (sample size n=10), while if to the question “how many times have you voted in your life?” we get an answer like “I’ve voted 10 times in my life” this comes from a single person (sample size n=1), so keep this in mind.



Why is the dispersion reported by a quasi-Poisson model different from residual deviance / residual df?
In BIO144 we check for overdispersion with the ratio of the residual deviance to the residual degrees of freedom. When you then fit a quasi-Poisson (or quasibinomial) model, summary() reports a “dispersion parameter” that is usually a bit different from that ratio. This is because R estimates the dispersion from the Pearson residuals, not the deviance residuals:
sum(residuals(my_quasi_model, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(my_quasi_model)
Both are reasonable ways to estimate the dispersion; they just use slightly different kinds of residuals. For example, in the Unit 8 grouse tick data the deviance ratio is about 8.6 and the quasi-Poisson dispersion is about 12.5. Either way, the data are clearly overdispersed.


How large does the dispersion have to be before I should worry?
Values above 1 mean overdispersion, but a little overdispersion is not a problem. The course book (Chapters 8 and 9) uses the rough guide that a ratio of residual deviance to residual degrees of freedom above about 1.5–2 suggests overdispersion that should be dealt with (for example with a quasi-Poisson or quasibinomial model). Like all rules of thumb, this is only a rough guide: how much overdispersion matters also depends on the sample size. Note that this check does not work for binary (0/1) data.


ANOVA or multiple regression?
ANOVA and (multiple) regression are both linear models, fitted in R with lm(). ANOVA is the special case in which all explanatory variables are categorical. The difference is mostly in which output we look at first:

For a categorical explanatory variable with k levels, we first look at the anova() table: one F-test of whether the group means differ at all. The summary() table instead gives k − 1 separate t-tests, each comparing one level with the reference level, which is usually not the question we want to answer first.
For a continuous explanatory variable, the summary() table directly gives the estimate of the slope and its test.

When a model has both kinds of explanatory variable, use both tables.


Degrees of freedom in a one-way ANOVA
With n observations in g groups: the total sum of squares has n − 1 degrees of freedom; the groups (the model) use g − 1; the residuals have n − g. The F-test uses g − 1 and n − g degrees of freedom. For example, 20 observations in 4 groups give F with 3 and 16 degrees of freedom. (Counting the intercept as well, the model estimates g parameters in total, which is why the residual df is n − g.) See “Degrees of freedom” in the course book, Chapters 3 and 5.


Does a t-test work when the two groups have different numbers of observations?
Yes. A t-test (or a linear model) does not need equal group sizes, as long as its assumptions are met and each group has enough observations. Unequal group sizes slightly reduce the precision of the estimate of the difference, compared with the same total split equally. With unequal variances as well, use var.equal = FALSE (Welch’s t-test), which estimates the variance separately in each group.
It is often more important to ask why the group sizes differ. In the class reaction time data, for example, if people of one sex at birth were more willing to take part than the other, the sample may not represent the class, whatever the test says.


What does “a distribution with a long tail of high values” mean?
It means that large values are more frequent than they would be in a symmetric distribution (such as the normal distribution): the distribution is right-skewed. The mean is pulled towards the high values more than the median is, so in such a distribution the mean is larger than the median.

Use R to fit linear mixed models with random intercepts, and with random slopes, using lmer() from the lme4 package.

Interpret mixed model output in biological terms, including what the variance components say about variation among groups.
Explain why degrees of freedom, and so p-values, for fixed effects in mixed models are not straightforward, and that several approximations exist (e.g. Satterthwaite’s method).
Identify limitations and assumptions of mixed models in a described analysis.
Recognise a correct and complete statement of results from a mixed model.

Chapter 11.2: What next?
After this unit, students will be able to:

Describe which kinds of data the methods in BIO144 can analyse: data that meet the assumptions of linear models, count and binary data using generalised linear models, grouped or repeated-measures data using mixed models, and many variables at once using ordination.
Explain why data collected over time or across space often violate the assumption of independent observations, and so require specialised methods (time series analysis, spatial analysis).
Recognise features of a research question or dataset that call for methods beyond BIO144, such as non-independent observations, non-linear relationships, abrupt changes in a relationship, many interrelated variables, time-to-event responses, or results from multiple studies.
Match a described research situation to a suitable family of methods: time series analysis, spatial analysis, non-linear regression, breakpoint analysis, generalised additive models, structural equation modelling, machine learning, meta-analysis, survival analysis, non-parametric methods, power analysis or Bayesian statistics.
Explain why the analysis, including the sample size needed (power analysis), should be planned when the study is designed.
Explain why the choice of analysis should be driven by the research question rather than by the techniques available.

Learning objectives
These learning objectives, together with the content of the course book chapter, define what you need to know for the exam.
After this unit, students will be able to:

Write a planning sentence for a described study, stating the question, the type of response variable, the data structure, the explanatory variables, the planned model and the expected residual degrees of freedom.
Choose a model (linear model, binomial GLM, Poisson GLM, mixed model or ordination) from the type of response variable, the explanatory variables and the data structure of a described study.
Identify the experimental unit in a described study, and recognise pseudoreplication.
Explain the roles of replication, randomisation, controls, blocking and balance in study design.
Count the parameters a planned model will estimate, calculate the expected residual degrees of freedom, and judge whether they are enough.
Explain how sample size affects the precision of estimates and the power of a study, and what a power analysis is for.
Decide which terms to include in a model from the question and the design (variables of interest, planned interactions, design variables, potential confounders), and explain why trying many models or using stepwise selection gives misleading p-values.
Check a fitted model before interpreting it, make explicit predictions from it, and plot the predictions together with the data.
Recognise a report that gives both the statistical result and its biological meaning.
